messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kofi's Vigil

Kofi was twenty-five when the officers stopped him on Nostrand Avenue in Brooklyn on a March evening. He had been working as a freelance journalist for eighteen months, building a reputation covering community policing and housing inequality in neighborhoods where he had grown up. That night, he was returning from an interview in Brownsville, his camera bag slung across his chest, his phone still recording audio notes. The officers said later they were responding to reports of a robbery in the area. Kofi was the right height, the right build, the right color in the wrong place at the wrong moment.

What happened over the next forty minutes existed in his memory now as a series of hyperreal, fractured images: the sudden shouting, the hands on his jacket, the officer's face inches from his own, the sound of his camera hitting the pavement. He remembered the weight of the officer's knee, the taste of concrete, the officer's radio crackling with static and voices. He remembered the exact pitch of the dispatcher's voice coming through the speaker clipped to the officer's shoulder—a particular timbre that his brain had apparently recorded with photographic precision. He had been released without charges. The investigation found no wrongdoing.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi returned to work, but something fundamental had shifted. He began wearing larger, darker clothes—hoodies even in warmer weather, oversized jackets that made him less visible, less of a shape that could be mistaken for anything. At the newspaper's offices in Midtown, he found himself unable to concentrate on assignments. His editor had asked him to write a piece on stop-and-frisk patterns, a topic he had been eager to pursue, but when he sat at his desk the words dissolved. He could not finish sentences. The narrative fragments scattered. He realized he was no longer the person who had wanted to tell these stories.

The footsteps became the worst part. In the hallways of the office building, on the subway platform, on the street outside his apartment—any footsteps behind him triggered an immediate, visceral response. He would turn, scan, try to assess the threat. His girlfriend, Maya, had mentioned it after he'd done it three times during a walk to dinner. He had not realized he was doing it. Now he was acutely aware of it, unable to stop, certain that the moment he stopped checking was the moment something would happen again.

Certain songs would arrive without warning on his Spotify mix or in a bodega, and suddenly he was back on Nostrand Avenue—the memory more vivid and present than his current surroundings, the officer's voice not just remembered but heard, playing inside his head with startling clarity. He had come to avoid music almost entirely, deleting playlists, asking friends not to play anything when he was around. But this created a strange isolation. He had loved music. He had been someone who could describe a song and make people understand why it mattered. Now he was someone who flinched at sound.

He began declining invitations. Unfamiliar places felt unmanageable—he could not map the exits, could not predict where danger might come from. His world contracted. He avoided his mother's church because it reminded him of his uncle, who had been killed by police in 2015, and grief was something he could not afford to feel. He avoided his favorite coffee shop because the owner had asked him about his assignment, and the conversation had nearly broken him open. He avoided positive feelings because they felt dangerous, a betrayal of something, or a setup for loss. He had become someone who moved through the world trying not to feel anything at all.

By late autumn, seven months after the stop, Maya had stopped asking when he would be ready to talk about it. His editor had stopped assigning him stories. He had come to believe that his life had been fundamentally destroyed, that he was no longer capable of being a journalist or a partner or the person he had been. The hypervigilance, the avoidance, the way his own memories had become more real than his present moment—all of it had accumulated into a conviction that he would never be okay again.

It was Maya who finally insisted he see someone. She had found a therapist who worked with trauma. Kofi had resisted, certain that talking would only make things worse, that it would confirm what he already knew about himself. But he was exhausted. He was losing everything. He called the office and made an appointment, and for the first time since March, he allowed himself to hope that something might change.
